summary: Defines an RTP header extension in which an audio stream's packets say how loud their audio sample is. In large conferences, a mixer can use it to forward only the loudest streams without decoding every stream.

eli5.summary: In a big group call, the system only needs to pick whoever is talking. If each voice packet has a loudness note, it can skip opening all of them.

questions: how mixers detect who is speaking
what is the rtp audio level header extension
how do mixers pick the loudest speaker
subtitle: A tiny RTP header extension that tells a conference mixer how loud each audio packet is, so it need not decode them all.

tldr.problem: An audio mixer in a large conference must decode and measure many streams to pick the few loudest to forward, which limits how large a conference it can support.
tldr.mechanism: Each sender adds a one-byte RTP header extension carrying the packet's audio level in -dBov (0 to 127) and an optional voice activity flag called V.
tldr.outcome: The mixer can choose which streams to forward from the header alone, without decoding every stream.

today: RFC 6464 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion for the opposite direction, mixer to client, is RFC 6465.

sections.title: The Mixer Workload Problem
sections.content:
In a centralized RTP audio conference, a mixer or forwarder receives audio streams from many or all participants and selectively forwards some of them. In a large conference only a few streams are meant to be forwarded.

To choose, the server needs to decode, measure audio levels and possibly run voice activity detection on a large number of streams, and that processing limits the size or number of conferences it can support. This RFC defines an RTP header extension (the general mechanism of RFC 5285) through which senders indicate the audio level of each packet's payload. It is different from, but complementary with, RFC 6465, where mixers tell clients the levels of the sources that made up the mixed audio.
sections.eli5: A teacher choosing who is talking loudest does not need to listen to every child's whole speech if each child holds up a loudness card.

sections.title: The Audio Level Extension
sections.content:
The extension element is a single byte, carried with either the one-byte or two-byte header form from RFC 5285. In the one-byte form the length field is 0, meaning one byte follows. In the two-byte form the length field is 1 and a padding byte of 0 follows the data byte.

The most significant bit is the flag V. The other seven bits hold the audio level, with the least significant bit of the level in the least significant bit of the byte.
sections.eli5: The note is one small byte: one bit says 'someone seems to be talking' and the other seven bits say how loud.

sections.title: How the Level Is Measured
sections.content:
The level is expressed in -dBov, with values 0 to 127 representing 0 to -127 dBov. dBov is the level in decibels relative to the overload point of the system, the highest-intensity signal the payload format can encode. This is useful for digital implementations because the analog calibration need not be known.

Digital silence, for example a muted source, MUST be represented as 127, whatever the dynamic range of the format. The value covers only the audio in that packet, with no long-term averaging or smoothing, and it is measured as a root mean square of all the samples the packet encodes. For payloads with error-correction or loss-concealment data, the level reflects normal decoding only. With redundant audio (RFC 2198), the header describes the primary encoding. The level is defined the same way as the noise level byte in the comfort noise payload of RFC 3389.

The V bit optionally says whether the encoder believes the packet contains voice activity: 1 means yes and 0 means no. The detection algorithm is left implementation-specific. If V is not in use, its value is unspecified and receivers MUST ignore it.
sections.eli5: Zero means as loud as the equipment can possibly go, and bigger numbers mean quieter. A silent microphone says 127.

sections.title: Signaling in SDP
sections.content:
The extension is declared in an SDP extmap attribute using the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ssrc-audio-level. It has one extension attribute, vad, set to on or off. With vad=on the V bit is in use and senders MUST set it. With vad=off the bit is not in use and receivers MUST ignore it. If the attribute is not given, the default is vad=on.

An example line is a=extmap:6 urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ssrc-audio-level vad=on. The attribute only controls this extension and says nothing about other voice activity features such as discontinuous transmission, comfort noise or silence suppression.

An endpoint MAY signal several instances of the extension with different vad values, as long as they use different identifiers. Within an RTP session, the semantics for a given identifier MUST NOT change.
sections.eli5: Before the call, each side says 'I will include loudness notes, and I will also say whether I think it is speech.'

sections.title: Using the Levels Sensibly
sections.content:
This non-normative section advises mixers not to base forwarding decisions on single-packet levels. Levels should be measured over longer intervals, with some low-pass filtering, so a cough or a dropped microphone is not mistaken for speech. That filtering has to be balanced against clipping the start of a speaker's speech.

Participants may also have different input settings, so some automatic gain control may help, for example by measuring peak levels, average levels during speech, or background levels during non-speech. The same advice applies whether levels come from endpoints or are calculated at the server.
sections.eli5: Do not pick the speaker from one loud sound. Wait a moment to be sure it is really someone talking.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious endpoint could set the values falsely. Claiming audio is present, or exaggerating levels, could mount a denial-of-service attack by sending silence to suppress other members' audio, or could let it dominate the conference by seizing the speaker-selection algorithm. A device relying on untrusted endpoints SHOULD periodically audit the transmitted levels. Some discrepancy is not proof of malice, because an endpoint may measure levels before encoding.

In SRTP, header extensions are authenticated but not encrypted, so a passive observer can see the levels packet by packet and might infer information about the conversation, possibly with phoneme-level resolution. Where this is a concern, additional mechanisms MUST be used to protect confidentiality, such as header extension encryption or a lower-level mechanism like IPsec.
sections.eli5: Someone could shout 'I am loudest!' falsely, so the mixer should check now and then. Also, anyone peeking at the loudness notes can learn a bit about the conversation.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers the extension URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ssrc-audio-level, described as Audio Level, in the RTP Compact Header Extensions subregistry of the RTP Parameters registry.
sections.eli5: The extension's name is written in an official list so everyone uses the same one.
